content: 1. Nafcillin interacts with hepatic and intestinal enzyme CYP3A4 metabolism. When co-administered with strong CYP3A4 inducers for more than 14 days, consider increasing the dose of vilazodone up to twofold, but do not exceed 80 mg/day. Monitor the patient closely. 2. Nafcillin reduces the levels or effects of vinblastine, vincristine, vincristine liposomal, and vinorelbine by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. These interactions are considered minor, and their clinical significance is unknown. 3. Nafcillin significantly decreases the levels or effects of voclosporin, vonoprazan, vorapaxar, and voxilaprevir by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid co-administration or use alternative drugs. 4. Nafcillin decreases voriconazole levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Modify therapy and monitor closely. 5. Nafcillin reduces vortioxetine levels by increasing its metabolism. Modify therapy and monitor closely. 6. Nafcillin decreases warfarin levels by mechanisms involving CYP3A4 and other enzymes. Monitor INR more frequently and adjust the warfarin dose as needed. 7. Nafcillin interacts with willow bark by decreasing renal clearance, potentially increasing levels of either substance. Use caution and monitor closely. 8. Nafcillin decreases zanubrutinib levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid co-administration or use alternative drugs. If unavoidable, increase zanubrutinib dose to 320 mg twice daily and resume the previous dose after discontinuing the CYP3A4 inducer. 9. Nafcillin reduces the levels or effects of ziprasidone, zolpidem, and zonisamide by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. These interactions are minor, and their clinical significance is unknown. 10. Nafcillin decreases zuranolone levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid co-administration or use alternative drugs. 11. Nafcillin may cause hypersensitivity reactions, including anaphylaxis, neutropenia, interstitial nephritis, hypokalemia, neurotoxicity (at high doses), pseudomembranous colitis, and phlebitis. Use oxacillin in pediatric patients to reduce the risk of phlebitis. 12. Patients with a history of hypersensitivity to penicillins or cephalosporins, or those with multiple allergen sensitivities, are at higher risk for severe allergic reactions. Discontinue nafcillin immediately if an allergic reaction occurs and initiate appropriate therapy. 13. Nafcillin is primarily cleared through the liver and biliary tract. Exercise caution in patients with concurrent hepatic insufficiency and renal dysfunction. 14. Prolonged use of nafcillin may lead to overgrowth of non-susceptible organisms. If new infections occur, discontinue the drug and take appropriate measures. 15. Monitor renal, hepatic, and hematologic systems periodically during prolonged treatment. High doses of nafcillin may cause elevations in liver transaminases and/or cholestasis. Perform baseline and periodic assessments of liver and kidney function. 16. Nafcillin-associated nephrotoxicity, including renal tubular damage and interstitial nephritis, may manifest as hematuria, proteinuria, and acute kidney injury. Most cases resolve upon discontinuation, but some may require dialysis or result in permanent renal damage. 17. Nafcillin is classified as Pregnancy Category B. It is excreted in breast milk, so use caution in breastfeeding mothers. 18. Nafcillin is metabolized primarily in the liver and excreted via the liver and kidneys. It induces hepatic CYP3A4 enzymes. 19. Nafcillin is available in injectable forms, including 1 g, 2 g, 10 g, 20 mg/mL, and 2 g/100 mL preparations. It is administered intramuscularly or intravenously. 20. Common side effects include pain, swelling, and inflammation at the injection site, as well as rash. Serious side effects include severe allergic reactions, seizures, kidney damage, liver damage, antibiotic-associated diarrhea, and blood disorders such as agranulocytosis and neutropenia. 21. Patients should inform their healthcare provider of all health conditions, medications, and supplements before using nafcillin. This includes allergies to penicillin, other medications, or corn products, as well as a history of asthma, liver or kidney disease, or antibiotic-associated diarrhea. 22. There are no known interactions between nafcillin and food or drinks. However, heavy alcohol consumption may impair the immune response and hinder infection recovery. 23. Nafcillin may interact with other medications, including tetracyclines, warfarin, cyclosporine, and others. Always inform your healthcare provider about all medications and supplements being used to avoid potential interactions.
